new.title: Peek inside the Kruisheren monastery hotel
new.desc: One of the few fully preserved Gothic monasteries in the Netherlands, where Crosier monks once copied and bound books. Since the 2000s it has been a design hotel, with modern furniture set under late medieval vaults.
new.tip: You do not need to stay the night: walk into the former church, now the lobby and wine bar, and look up at the vaults and the mezzanine built inside them.

new.title: Light a candle for the Sterre der Zee
new.desc: The Romanesque Onze Lieve Vrouwebasiliek has a fortress-like westwork, but most people come for the side chapel with the medieval statue of the Sterre der Zee (Star of the Sea), the city's beloved patroness. Locals still drop in to light a candle.
new.tip: After the chapel, step into the quiet cloister; the treasury off the eastern walk holds reliquaries that survived the French period.

new.title: Get the whole city story at the Maastricht Museum
new.desc: A compact museum upstairs in Centre Céramique that runs from prehistoric finds to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty. The local ceramics collection, from the factories that gave the Sphinx and Céramique districts their names, is a highlight.
new.tip: Pick the audio tour in Mestreechs, the city dialect, just to hear how it sounds; an English version is available too.

new.title: Roam the ramparts of the Frontenpark
new.desc: An unpolished 20-hectare park on the old northern fortifications, where sheep graze the grassy bastions of the Hoge Fronten. Steel walkways, the round Gashouder and De Krul, a leftover curl of a demolished bridge ramp, give it an industrial edge.
new.tip: Climb onto the Hoge Fronten for a wide view over the city, then finish at the Radium and Gashouder side by the Sphinx district.

new.title: Hike up to the Lichtenberg ruins
new.desc: The ruined castle of Lichtenberg sits on the edge of the Sint-Pietersberg, high above the Maas. Walls and a tower stump frame views over the river valley and the Belgian border.
new.tip: Walk up from the Jeker side of town past Fort Sint Pieter; the ruins are usually open from spring to autumn and a seasonal restaurant sits right beside them.

new.title: Lunch in the garden of Marres Kitchen
new.desc: Marres, a house for contemporary culture in the former home of an old Maastricht brewing family, hides a walled city garden behind it. Its restaurant is one of the calmest places to eat in the centre.
new.tip: Ask for a table in the garden on a sunny day, then look around the exhibition rooms upstairs.

new.title: Drink Limburg wine on the Bredestraat
new.desc: Wijnrestaurant Mes Amis builds its dishes around wines from Limburg's own vineyards, and Goesting next door sells only Limburg bottles. A local's favourite pairing for anyone who doubts Dutch wine.
new.tip: Ask the staff to pour something from a small Heuvelland producer you would never find elsewhere, then pick up a bottle next door.

new.title: Graze the Friday market on the Markt
new.desc: On Wednesdays and Fridays the square in front of the stadhuis fills with market stalls. Friday is the big one, with cheese, Limburg sausage, fish and vlaai drawing shoppers from across the border.
new.tip: Go early on Friday morning, grab something hot from a fish stall and eat it by the Minckelers statue.

new.title: Toast with a local beer at Café de Zwaan
new.desc: A grand old café-restaurant on the Markt, facing the 17th-century stadhuis. It is a good place to try beers from the Limburg breweries alongside a proper meal.
new.tip: Sit on the terrace in the late afternoon when the sun hits the town hall façade.

new.title: Have a drink in the quay cellars of 't Bassin
new.desc: Maastricht's old inner harbour, now a marina, is lined with former wharf cellars turned into cafés, restaurants and galleries. Boats bob right in front of the terraces.
new.tip: Hire a small sloop here and putter out onto the Maas for an hour before your drink.

new.title: Lunch below Château Neercanne
new.desc: This castle sits on a terrace cut into the Cannerberg, with baroque gardens stepping down to the Jeker valley and its own small vineyard. Wine is stored in a marl cave right behind the house.
new.tip: For a relaxed visit, choose the lunch restaurant L'Auberge in the former stables, then stroll the terraced garden.

new.title: Crawl through the Kazematten
new.desc: Between the 16th and 19th centuries soldiers dug kilometres of tunnels under the west of the city to ambush attackers underground. Listening galleries and gun ports are still there, and people sheltered here in the Second World War.
new.tip: Entry is by guided tour only, starting from the Waldeckpark; it is cold down there, so bring a jumper.

new.title: Tour the last old brewery of Maastricht
new.desc: Brouwerij Bosch in Wyck stopped brewing in 1970 but kept its 19th-century steam machinery and five-storey malt house intact. Of the 28 breweries the city had around 1900, it is the only one left.
new.tip: Book a guided tour; it ends with a beer tasting in one of the old halls.

new.title: Sail up the Maas into Belgium
new.desc: Riverboats leave from the Maaspromenade for trips upstream, past the Sint-Pietersberg and on into Belgium. Seeing the marl cliffs and the ENCI quarry from the water puts the city in a new light.
new.tip: Pick a trip that goes through the locks towards Belgium rather than the short city loop.

new.title: Waltz along with André Rieu on the Vrijthof
new.desc: Every summer Maastricht's own violinist plays a run of open-air concerts on the Vrijthof. Even without a ticket, the whole square becomes a party, with terraces full and music drifting over the rooftops.
new.tip: No ticket? Book a table on one of the café terraces around the square, where you can hear and partly see the show.

new.title: Explore Kasteel Hoensbroek in Heerlen
new.desc: One of the largest castles in the Netherlands, a moated complex of four wings grown around a 14th-century round tower. Dozens of halls and rooms show its six centuries as the seat of the Hoensbroeck family.
new.tip: Climb the round tower for a view over the former mining region; Hoensbroek has its own train station a short walk away.

new.title: See the Glaspaleis and murals of Heerlen
new.desc: Heerlen's Glaspaleis, a 1935 department store with glass walls on three sides, is an icon of early modernism and now houses SCHUNCK. Around it, the city has filled its walls with more than a hundred murals since 2013.
new.tip: Download the free Street Art Cities app to follow the murals, and walk up SCHUNCK's painted staircase, which is free to see.

new.title: Descend into the crypt of Rolduc in Kerkrade
new.desc: Rolduc, founded by Augustinian monks in 1104, is one of the largest abbey complexes in the Netherlands. Its clover-leaf Romanesque crypt from 1108 has columns that are each carved differently.
new.tip: The abbey also has a tasting room for Rolduc beer; combine it with a ride on the Miljoenenlijn, which stops in Kerkrade.

new.title: Find the scandalous murals of Wahlwiller
new.desc: In 1946 Aad de Haas covered the little Sint-Cunibertuskerk in Wahlwiller with expressive paintings. His Stations of the Cross caused such a row that they were removed in 1949, only to return to the church after its restoration around 1980.
new.tip: The village lies on the road between Gulpen and Vaals; combine it with a walk through the surrounding orchards.

new.title: Walk the old fortress town of Sittard
new.desc: Sittard's Markt, laid out around 1300, is ringed by half-timbered houses and terraces, with the 80-metre tower of the Grote Kerk rising behind it. Quiet lanes, monastery gardens and remains of the walls surround the centre.
new.tip: Sittard station is a short walk from the Markt; follow the Kerkepad past the Sint-Michielskerk before sitting down on a terrace.

new.title: Visit the mission village of Steyl near Venlo
new.desc: Steyl, on the Maas just south of Venlo, is a village of monasteries founded by Saint Arnold Janssen. Its Missiemuseum, barely changed since the early 1900s, is crammed with objects missionaries sent home from around the world.
new.tip: Wander the Jochumhof botanical garden too, then take the little ferry across the Maas to Baarlo.

new.title: Look up at the Renaissance stadhuis of Venlo
new.desc: Venlo's late 16th-century town hall stands in the middle of the Markt, its façade decorated with medallions of famous townspeople. Nearby Gasthuisstraat is one of the most medieval streets in the country.
new.tip: Afterwards find the bronze köpkes, little heads of local characters, along the Keizerstraat, known locally as Floddergats.

new.title: Spot half-timbered farms around Epen
new.desc: The upper Geul valley around Epen, Mechelen and Cottessen is the most hilly and rural corner of the Netherlands, dotted with white half-timbered farmhouses, some from the 15th century. Locals call it the prettiest stretch of the Heuvelland.
new.tip: Walk the lanes between Epen and Mechelen or up to the hamlet of Camerig for the best clusters of vakwerk houses.

new.title: Refuel at the 'mountain hut' in the Vijlenerbos
new.desc: Boscafé 't Hijgend Hert, deep in the beech woods near Vijlen, calls itself the only mountain hut in the Netherlands. There has been a café here since 1933, and it now brews its own Hert beer.
new.tip: Walk in from Vijlen or the parking area on the Epenerbaan; huge slices of vlaai are the reward.

new.title: Eat Limburg asparagus in season in Venlo
new.desc: The sandy soils of Noord-Limburg grow the region's famous white asparagus. In spring it appears on every menu and is sold from stalls along the country roads.
new.tip: Order it the classic way, with ham, egg and melted butter, or buy a bundle at the Venlo weekmarkt to cook yourself.

new.title: Taste Alfa beer at its brewery in Thull
new.desc: Alfa is a small independent family brewery in the hamlet of Thull near Schinnen, and its beers have collected gold awards. A taste of Limburg brewing far from the big names.
new.tip: Check the brewery website for tour days; a visit fits neatly into a bike ride between Valkenburg and Sittard.

new.title: Eat pancakes at the Jachthut op den Hamert
new.desc: A pancake restaurant in a hunting lodge on the edge of the river dunes of De Hamert, near Wellerlooi in Noord-Limburg. It is the classic start and finish of walks through the Maasduinen.
new.tip: Earn your pancake first: do one of the marked dune loops that begin right outside, then sit down with muddy boots.

new.title: Ride the steam train on the Miljoenenlijn
new.desc: The 'Million Line' got its name because its tunnels, cuttings and high embankments through the mining region cost a fortune in the 1930s. Volunteers now run steam and vintage trains between Kerkrade and Schin op Geul.
new.tip: Start in Simpelveld, the railway's home base with its museum and old station; trains run mainly from spring to autumn.

new.title: Walk the river dunes of De Hamert
new.desc: National Park De Maasduinen holds the longest belt of river dunes in the Netherlands. At Landgoed De Hamert, trails cross drifting sand, heath and fens, past a Bronze Age burial mound.
new.tip: Marked loops of different lengths start from the information board at the Jachthut; bus 83 between Venlo and Nijmegen stops at Wellerlooi.

new.title: Stroll the Kasteeltuinen of Arcen
new.desc: More than fifteen gardens, from Renaissance parterres to ponds and rose beds, are laid out around a 17th-century castle in the Maas village of Arcen. One of the most varied garden parks in Europe.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk through Arcen's old centre on the Maas; in late November the park hosts a Christmas fair.

new.title: Go down the coal mine in Valkenburg
new.desc: Since 1917 a former marl quarry under Valkenburg has been dressed up as a coal mine, filled with real machines from the Limburg pits that closed in the 1970s. Guides, some of them ex-miners, tell what life underground was like.
new.tip: Tours leave every hour; it stays around 15 degrees below ground, so bring a layer.

new.title: Rock out at Pinkpop in Landgraaf
new.desc: Pinkpop, held around Pentecost in Landgraaf, is a multi-day rock festival with a history going back to 1970. For a few days the former mining town fills with tents and big names.
new.tip: Tickets sell fast; if you skip the camping, Landgraaf and Heerlen stations are the nearest rail stops.

new.title: Cycle the Voerstreekroute from Slenaken
new.desc: From the Gulp valley at Slenaken this route crosses into the Belgian Voerstreek, a quieter patchwork of small hills, orchards and sunken lanes with views at every crest.
new.tip: Expect real climbs on the way back into the Netherlands; an e-bike from Slenaken or Gulpen makes it relaxed.
